statements.action_statement: Fix pending: the next upstream Caddy release built with Go 1.26.9+ and golang.org/x/net 0.60.0+ (the image moves to it the week it is published). Until then keep port 8443 on your LAN or VPN, as the self-hosting guide says: the issue is a denial of service of the HTTP/2 server by a client that can reach it.
statements.status_notes: net/http and x/net/http2 denial of service; Caddy serves HTTP/2 on 8443. Decided by maintainer.

statements.action_statement: Fix pending: the next upstream Caddy release built with Go 1.26.9+. Denial of service of the HTTP server through crafted Range headers; keep port 8443 on your LAN or VPN until then.

Fix pending: the next upstream Caddy release built with Go 1.26.9+. Denial of service of the TLS server through multiple ECH outer extensions in a ClientHello; keep port 8443 on your LAN or VPN until then.

statements.impact_statement: crypto/x509's chain verification with untrusted intermediates runs when a Go program verifies a peer's certificate as a TLS client. Caddy in this image never does: deploy/Caddyfile sets auto_https off (no ACME), serves its own certificate from /data/certs, and proxies to plain-http upstreams on localhost (reverse_proxy to the Flask backend and the central server); it verifies no certificate. The fix (Go 1.26.10) arrives with the next Caddy release anyway.

This is pip's vendored urllib3 (pip/_vendor/urllib3, pip 26.2.2's vendor.txt), imported by pip alone; pip runs only during the image build. The application and its packages import the urllib3 that backend/requirements.lock installs (2.8.0, which has the fix), never pip's copy. The HTTPS-proxy TLS override needs an HTTPS proxy configured for a running urllib3, which the image has nowhere.

pip's vendored urllib3 (pip/_vendor), imported by pip alone, which runs only while the image is built; the application's urllib3 is 2.8.0 from backend/requirements.lock, where the chunked-encoding fix is in.

pip's vendored msgpack (pip/_vendor/msgpack), which pip uses for its HTTP cache during an install; pip runs only while the image is built. Nothing in backend/requirements.lock depends on msgpack and the application never imports it, so no Unpacker is ever reused on untrusted data at runtime.

setuptools' PackageIndex.download is the easy_install-era downloader, run only by setup.py-driven installs that fetch distributions by URL. No setuptools module is importable by either interpreter in the image (the application's /opt/app-root/bin/python and the system python3.14 both answer ModuleNotFoundError, checked in the built image): the scanner's hit is package metadata of the base image's build tooling, not an installed package, and the application installs nothing at runtime.
